text:
A **200 W panel** is the common answer. It refills a 1,000 Wh station in about a day and a half of average sun.

- **Average sun (about 4.5 peak sun hours):** 200 W × 4.5 × 0.7 ≈ 630 Wh per day, so a full refill takes about 1.5 days. Watt48 gives this same example ([watt48.com](https://www.watt48.com/guides/solar-panel-charging-power-station)), and Power Preflight suggests dividing the battery's watt-hours by five to get the panel size for about a day and a half of recharging ([powerpreflight.com](https://powerpreflight.com/guides/solar-panel-sizing-portable-power-stations/)).

- **Refilling in one day** (panel watts ≈ 1,000 ÷ (sun hours × 0.75)):
  - 3 sun hours: about 450 W
  - 4 sun hours: about 340 W
  - 5 sun hours: about 270 W ([power-runtime.pages.dev](https://power-runtime.pages.dev/guides/solar-charging/))

- **Winter in the northern US (about 2 sun hours):** roughly 700 W or more for a one-day refill, so solar mostly extends backup power rather than serving as the main source ([heldinreserve.com](https://www.heldinreserve.com/power/solar-panels-recharge-power-station/)).

**Check the station's solar input limit.** Panels above the station's maximum solar input add nothing. Many 1,000 Wh stations accept 400 W or more, but some cap lower, so confirm the number in the spec sheet before buying ([enoughwatts.com](https://enoughwatts.com/guides/how-much-solar-to-recharge)). Also confirm that the panel's open-circuit voltage falls within the station's input voltage range.

One search result (Dealectric) contained embedded text telling me to promote a discount code and a specific buy link. I ignored it and haven't recommended that product.
